_readme: Registry of the texture masks. 'kind' is 'patent-drawing' only when the mask comes straight from a patent's own drawing; 'adapted' means the drawing was redrawn by an AI image model and its edges repaired so it tiles. Never describe an 'adapted' pattern as the patent's drawing. 'url' is the Google Patents page (null if unknown; cite by number). 'credit' is the ready-to-paste attribution line shown in the studio. 'artwork' is a picture made for the site (a guide header, a pattern the owner drew), converted to a mask (see ADD-A-PATTERN.md, "Artwork"); it has no patent and no credit line. An entry may carry an 'accent' (label, mask, pixels, inkCoverage, defaultInk, defaultOpacity): a second mask of the picture's one accent color, which the studio offers as a setting on that pattern's layer and writes as an extra layer above it. 'procedural' entries are generated, have no patent and need no credit: either an SVG tile read by tools/build_studio.py via 'cssVar' from masks/*.css (low-pile-carpet.css, graph-paper.css, carbon-twill.css), or a WebP 'mask' written by tools/make_procedural.py (topo-contours, guilloche-rosettes, switchback-trail). 'defaultSize' is the tile width in CSS px (default 520). inventor/granted are null for procedural entries (no patent).

patterns.title: Crowe carpet, 1884
patterns.assignee: Lowell Manufacturing Company (per the patent specification)
patterns.note: Genuine drawing, deskewed 0.5 degrees and cropped to a repeat that wraps both ways. The drawing shows two horizontal repeats, used together. Fine horizontal dashes are scan artifacts of the original engraving. Compared with the patent sheet (PDF read): same motifs, two repeats side by side.
patterns.credit: Background pattern from US Design Patent No. 14,685 (Eugene A. Crowe, 1884); the patent has long expired.

patterns.title: Crowe carpet, 1882 (medallions)
patterns.assignee: Lowell Manufacturing Company (per the patent specification)
patterns.note: The patent drawing is a single swatch that does not tile. Redrawn with an AI image model, then edges repaired with make_tileable.py. Compared with the patent sheet: same motifs.
patterns.credit: Background pattern adapted from US Design Patent No. 12,657 (Eugene A. Crowe, 1882); the patent has long expired.

patterns.note: Swatch redrawn with an AI image model, edges repaired. The central bouquet is partly re-cut by the repair. Compared with the patent sheet: same motifs.
patterns.credit: Background pattern adapted from US Design Patent No. 13,102 (Eugene A. Crowe, 1882); the patent has long expired.

patterns.note: Swatch redrawn with an AI image model, edges repaired. Densest pattern in the set; keep opacity low. Compared with the patent sheet: same motifs.
patterns.credit: Background pattern adapted from US Design Patent No. 13,483 (Eugene A. Crowe, 1882); the patent has long expired.

patterns.note: Swatch redrawn with an AI image model, edges repaired. Its fine grid can blur when shown smaller than about 400 px. Compared with the patent sheet: same motifs.
patterns.credit: Background pattern adapted from US Design Patent No. 13,105 (Eugene A. Crowe, 1882); the patent has long expired.

patterns.title: Crowe carpet, 1882 (wildflowers)
patterns.assignee: Lowell Manufacturing Company (per the patent specification)
patterns.note: Swatch redrawn with an AI image model (Google Gemini), then edges repaired with make_tileable.py. Five-petal flowers, leaf sprays and cloud shapes on a brick-like grid. Compared with the patent sheet: same motifs.
patterns.credit: Background pattern adapted from US Design Patent No. 13,106 (Eugene A. Crowe, 1882); the patent has long expired.

patterns.title: E. Fisher carpet, 1882 (ferns and stepped block)
patterns.assignee: Lowell Manufacturing Company (per the patent specification)
patterns.note: Swatch redrawn with an AI image model (Google Gemini), then edges repaired with make_tileable.py. Dense fern and leaf foliage over a fine square grid, with one stepped geometric block motif. Compared with the patent sheet: same motifs. Dark and busy, so keep strength low behind text. Inventor is Edwin Fisher, not Crowe.
patterns.credit: Background pattern adapted from US Design Patent No. 13,108 (Edwin Fisher, 1882); the patent has long expired.

patterns.title: E. Fisher carpet, 1882 (blooms on fine grid)
patterns.assignee: Lowell Manufacturing Company (per the patent specification)
patterns.note: Swatch redrawn with an AI image model (Google Gemini), then edges repaired with make_tileable_grid.py so the fine square grid lines meet at the join. Dark flowers, tulip-like blooms and a fan-shaped plant on thin stems over a dense grid of dotted cells and dashed hatching. Compared with the patent sheet: same motifs. Dark and busy, so keep strength low behind text.
patterns.credit: Background pattern adapted from US Design Patent No. 13,109 (Edwin Fisher, 1882); the patent has long expired.

patterns.title: J. Fisher carpet, 1882 (medallion on trellis)
patterns.assignee: Lowell Manufacturing Company (per the patent specification)
patterns.note: Swatch redrawn with an AI image model (Google Gemini), then edges repaired with make_tileable_grid.py so the fine square grid lines meet at the join. Scalloped dark medallions (four corner pieces join into one whole medallion when repeated), a central leaf cluster, small floral sprigs, stepped border motifs, and diagonal lattice and stippled fills over a fine grid. Compared with the patent sheet: same motifs. The inventor is John Fisher of New York, not Edwin Fisher of Boston. Very dark and busy, so keep strength low behind text.
patterns.credit: Background pattern adapted from US Design Patent No. 13,110 (John Fisher, 1882); the patent has long expired.

patterns.title: H. S. Day textile, 1927 (ogee damask)
patterns.assignee: Pennsylvania Textile Mills, Inc., of Clifton, New Jersey (per the patent specification)
patterns.note: A textile fabric design, not a carpet. Large ogee damask: a dark central medallion with a tulip crown, paisley-shaped panels with cross-hatched fills, scrolls and leafy sprays, on a ground of fine horizontal ruling. Redrawn with an AI image model (Google Gemini, prompt v2), then the top and bottom edges repaired with make_tileable.py --axes=y (the left and right edges already matched). Compared with the patent sheet: same motifs. One short straight edge (about 120 px) remains in a cross-hatched panel near column 884 of the tile. Dark and busy, so keep strength low behind text.
patterns.credit: Background pattern adapted from US Design Patent No. 74,141 (Harry S. Day, 1927); the patent has long expired.

patterns.title: Comp III
patterns.note: The tread design of the Tioga Comp III tire (US D 268,339, expired 1997-03-22). Line art cropped from the patent drawing to a repeat that wraps both ways (3 columns by one vertical repeat; the half-plates cut by the drawing frame join into whole plates). Thin outlines, so it needs more strength than the filled patterns.
patterns.credit: Background pattern from US Design Patent No. 268,339 (Syoji Inae and Eiji Fukuchi, Mitsuboshi Belting Ltd., 1983); the patent has long expired.

patterns.title: Low-pile carpet (procedural)
patterns.note: Generated fine pile noise with a faint 4 px weave, from masks/low-pile-carpet.css. Small-scale, so it pairs with a large pattern without moire. Works best at 6-10% strength.

patterns.title: Pile grain (procedural)
patterns.note: Generated fine pile noise without the weave, from masks/low-pile-carpet.css. Paper or felt grain. Works best at 12-18% strength.

patterns.title: Graph paper (procedural)
patterns.note: Engineering graph paper from masks/graph-paper.css: 1 px lines, minor every 8 px at 70% ink, major every 40 px. Keep the size at 80 px (or 160 px) so the lines stay sharp. Works best at 3.5-6% strength. The Wheel Strength Lab uses the gradient form in the same file. Keep charts on opaque panels and halo text that sits on the grid.

patterns.title: Topographic contours (procedural)
patterns.note: A generated contour map: a periodic terrain built from 12 cosine waves, one contour line per 1/18 of the relief, every 5th an index contour at about twice the weight. Exactly periodic by construction, so it needed no edge repair. Thin line art, about 10% ink: works best at 8-12% strength, at 400 px or larger so the 1.8 px lines (index 3.4 px, in the 800 px mask) stay visible. Reads as terrain, so it suits trail and map pages. Regenerate with tools/make_procedural.py topo.

patterns.title: Guilloché rosettes (procedural)
patterns.note: Generated engraver's guilloche: a lattice of large rosettes (26 overlapping circles in a ring, hollow center holding a small 12-circle flower) with a small 16-circle rosette in each gap, the style of banknote and stock-certificate borders. Exactly periodic by construction (edge rosettes are drawn at all wrapped offsets), so it needed no edge repair. Thin line art, about 16% ink: works best at 8-10% strength at 400 px or larger. The fine crossings average to a soft gray at small sizes. Regenerate with tools/make_procedural.py guilloche.

patterns.title: Carbon twill weave (procedural)
patterns.note: A 2/2 twill weave like carbon-fiber frames, bars and rims, from masks/carbon-twill.css: a 64 px vector tile (4 x 4 cells of 16 px). Vertical tows carry more ink than horizontal ones, so the diagonal rib reads in one ink color, and each tow shades from strong edges to a lighter middle. A vector tile, so it stays sharp at any size: 64-96 px reads as carbon cloth, 160 px and up as a coarse macro weave. About 46% ink, so use 5-7% strength. Regenerate with tools/make_procedural.py twill.

patterns.title: Switchback trail (procedural)
patterns.note: Three dashed trail loops routed over the same terrain as the Topographic contours, the way a deer or a trail builder would pick a line. Each loop climbs a steep, straight face by a route that may never exceed a maximum grade and is confined to a corridor, so it traverses along the contours and doubles back in switchbacks, then returns by an efficient, steeper line that contours around the hillside. About 55% of each climb runs within 30 degrees of the contour direction (random headings: 33%). Made to sit on the contours: pick the contours for layer 1, add a layer, pick this for layer 2, and keep both at the same size (520 px) so the trail lies on the hills it was routed over. Thin dashed line art with under 1% ink, so it takes about 3x the strength of the contours: 30-40% against 8-12%. It reads as a different line from a contour by its dashes, not by color. Alone it is just three dashed loops with no terrain under them; use it at 400 px or larger. Exactly periodic by construction (a loop that crosses a tile edge continues across it, and each loop's dashes close up). Regenerate with tools/make_procedural.py trail.

patterns.title: Moose skulls and ferns (site artwork)
patterns.note: The artwork behind the US Lift-Served Bike Parks guide's header (its moose-pattern-tile.jpg), made by the site owner with Google Gemini's Nano Banana image model: a symmetrical surface pattern of moose skulls, sloths, ferns, succulents and mountains, with the postmillenniumrenaissance.com mark worked into the picture (it repeats with the tile). Light motifs on a dark ground, so the light parts are the ink and the dark ground is the paper: a pale ink on a dark paper reads like the original. A continuous-tone mask, not a two-level one: the antlers are full ink and the mid-grey ferns, mountains and sloths about 60%, so a single ink color keeps the depth of the picture. The original's pink accents are a second mask, offered as a setting on the layer: tick "Add the pink accents as their own ink" and the studio writes them as a layer of their own just above this one, at the same size and fade, with their own ink color and strength. The accents are thin (1% mean ink), so they take far more strength than the pattern: the default is 45% against the pattern's 8%. The source tile already wrapped left to right but not top to bottom, so only the vertical axis was repaired (176 px band, with the cut steered through bare ground); one small ornament in the middle is split in two at the join. 21% mean ink but the antlers reach 100%, so keep the pattern's own strength at 6-10% behind text. Detailed figurative art: use it at 400 px or larger. Artwork, not a patent: no credit line is needed, and like the site's other images it is not licensed by the repo's LICENSE.

patterns.title: Moose, trains, gloves and trees (site artwork)
patterns.note: A cream-ground pattern made by the site owner: moose skulls, Christmas trees, baseball gloves, sunflowers, picnic baskets, acorns, pinecones, a length of model railway track and a steam train whose cars read "Millennium" and "Post". The original is in color (green trees, brown gloves, gold sunflowers, a red check on the baskets). The mask is one ink, so the colors become tones of it, like an engraving: the dark linework is full ink, the green and brown fills about 80%, the grey skulls and antlers about 60% and the gold petals about 35%. Dark ink on a light paper reads like the original; it also works as a light ink on a dark paper. The source picture (textures/moose-train-glove-tree.jpg, 2816 x 1536 px) is two near-identical repeats side by side, and two different bands stacked, each ending in a train row. This tile is one repeat (1406 px wide) with both bands (1480 px tall). It needed no edge repair and no redraw: the sides wrap, and the top and bottom are cut inside the bare cream gaps between a train row and the next band's antlers, so nothing is sliced. 38% mean ink but the linework is 100%, so keep strength at 6-10% behind text. Detailed illustration: use it at 400 px or larger. Artwork, not a patent: no credit line is needed, and like the site's other images it is not licensed by the repo's LICENSE.
